III-C2 Channel Model

The links between the ground users and UAVs, as well as those between the UAV clusters and remote BS, follow a probabilistic line-of-sight (LoS) model. Specifically, the LoS probability between the uu-th ground user and the vv-th UAV is expressed as [37]:

Pu,vLoS=11+ψ​exp⁡[−β⁡(180π​arcsin⁡(Hu,vdu,v)−ψ)],P^{\mathrm{LoS}}_{u,v}=\frac{1}{1+\psi\exp\!\left[-\beta\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac{H_{u,v}}{d_{u,v}}\right)-\psi\right)\right]}, (6)

where ψ\psi and β\beta are environment-dependent constants. Moreover, Hu,vH_{u,v} and du,vd_{u,v} represent the vertical and total distances between the uu-th ground user and the vv-th UAV, respectively. Accordingly, the non-LoS (NLoS) probability is Pu,vNLoS=1−Pu,vLoSP^{\mathrm{NLoS}}_{u,v}=1-P^{\mathrm{LoS}}_{u,v}.

The path loss between the uu-th ground user and the vv-th UAV for LoS and NLoS links is as follows [37]:

Lu,vLoS=20​log⁡du,v+20​log⁡f+20​log⁡(4​π/c)+μLoS,L_{u,v}^{\text{LoS}}=20\log d_{u,v}+20\log f+20\log\left(4\pi/c\right)+\mu_{\text{LoS}}, (7)
Lu,vNLoS=20​log⁡du,v+20​log⁡f+20​log⁡(4​π/c)⏟free space path loss+μNLoS⏟excessivepath loss,L_{u,v}^{\text{NLoS}}=\underbrace{20\log d_{u,v}+20\log f+20\log\left(4\pi/c\right)}_{\text{free space path loss}}+\underbrace{\mu_{\text{NLoS}}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{excessive}\\ \text{path loss}\end{subarray}}, (8)

where μLoS\mu_{\mathrm{LoS}} and μNLoS\mu_{\mathrm{NLoS}} denote the excess path loss coefficients for LoS and NLoS links, respectively. Moreover, ff is frequency and cc represent light speed.

Accordingly, the average path loss between the uu-th ground user and the vv-th UAV is as follows [37]:

Lu,v=Pu,vLoS​Lu,vLoS+Pu,vNLoS​Lu,vNLoS.L_{u,v}=\mathit{P}^{\mathrm{LoS}}_{u,v}L_{u,v}^{\text{LoS}}+\mathit{P}^{\mathrm{NLoS}}_{u,v}L_{u,v}^{\text{NLoS}}. (9)

Note that the calculation of the average path loss Lc,bsL_{c,\mathrm{bs}} between the cc-th UAV cluster and remote BS follows the same procedure as described above.

III-C3 Transmission Model

In this part, we elaborate the transmission models for both ground user-to-UAV and UAV cluster-to-BS links.

1) Ground User-to-UAV Transmission Model. Each ground user may fall within the coverage areas of multiple UAVs. For simplicity, we assume that each ground user establishes a communication link with the geographically closest UAV. Specifically, the vu⋆v_{u}^{\star}-th UAV which is associated with the uu-th ground user is given as follows:

vu⋆=arg⁡minv∈𝒱⁡du,v.v_{u}^{\star}=\arg\min_{v\in\mathcal{V}}d_{u,v}. (10)

Accordingly, the SINR between the uu-th ground user and the vu⋆v_{u}^{\star}-th UAV is as follows [38]:

SINRu,vu⋆=Pu​10−Lu,vu⋆10∑u′∈𝒰vu⋆∖{u}Pu′​10−Lu′,vu⋆10+B​N0,\text{SINR}_{u,v_{u}^{\star}}=\frac{P_{u}10^{-\frac{L_{u,v_{u}^{\star}}}{10}}}{\sum_{u^{\prime}\in\mathcal{U}_{v_{u}^{\star}}\setminus\{u\}}P_{u^{\prime}}10^{-\frac{L_{u^{\prime},v_{u}^{\star}}}{10}}+BN_{0}}, (11)

where PuP_{u} is the transmit power of the uu-th ground user, BB denotes the channel bandwidth, and N0N_{0} is the noise power spectral density. Moreover, 𝒰vu⋆\mathcal{U}_{v_{u}^{\star}} denotes the set of ground users served by the vu⋆v_{u}^{\star}-th UAV.

Accordingly, the achievable transmission rate between the uu-th user and the selected vu⋆v_{u}^{\star}-th UAV is as follows [39]:

Ru,vu⋆=B​log2⁡(1+SINRu,vu⋆).R_{u,v_{u}^{\star}}=B\log_{2}\left(1+\text{SINR}_{u,v_{u}^{\star}}\right). (12)

2) UAV Cluster-to-BS Transmission Model. The BS is assumed to be equipped with multiple antennas, which enables it to distinguish signals originating from different UAV clusters. Consequently, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), rather than the SINR, is considered as the performance metric for the link between each cluster and BS. Specifically, the SNR between the cc-th UAV cluster and BS is as follows [40]:

SNRc,bs={Pc​Gc​10−Lc,bs10B​N0,if ​NVc≠1,Pv​10−Lc,bs10B​N0,if ​NVc=1,\text{SNR}_{c,\mathrm{bs}}=\begin{cases}\frac{P_{c}G_{c}10^{-\frac{L_{c,\textrm{bs}}}{10}}}{BN_{0}},&\text{if }N_{\mathrm{V}_{c}}\neq 1,\\ \frac{P_{v}10^{-\frac{L_{c,\textrm{bs}}}{10}}}{BN_{0}},&\text{if }N_{\mathrm{V}_{c}}=1,\end{cases} (13)

where PcP_{c} is the total transmit power of the cc-th UAV cluster, given by Pc=∑v=1NVc(wvc)2​PvP_{c}=\sum\nolimits_{v=1}^{N_{\mathrm{V}_{c}}}(w_{v_{c}})^{2}P_{v}, with PvP_{v} being the transmit power of a single UAV. Accordingly, the semantic transmission rate between the cc-th UAV cluster and BS is as follows [41]:

SRc,bs=B​Ikc,bs​L​ξc,bs​{kc,bs,SNRc,bs},\text{SR}_{c,\mathrm{bs}}=\frac{BI}{k_{c,\mathrm{bs}}L}\xi_{c,\mathrm{bs}}\{k_{c,\mathrm{bs}},\text{SNR}_{c,\mathrm{bs}}\}, (14)

where II and LL represent the expected number of semantic information and words per sentence, respectively. Moreover, kc,bsk_{c,\mathrm{bs}} denotes the average number of semantic symbols used per word in the cc-th cluster. In addition, ξc,bs\xi_{c,\mathrm{bs}} is the resulting semantic similarity between the cc-th UAV cluster and BS, which is determined as a function of both kc,bsk_{c,\mathrm{bs}} and SNRc,bs\text{SNR}_{c,\mathrm{bs}}.

III-D Energy Consumption Model

In this subsection, we present the flight energy consumption of UAVs. Specifically, for the vv-th UAV in the cc-th cluster, flying at a horizontal speed of VvcxyV_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}}, the propulsion power consumption is as follows [42], [43]:

Pvcxy​(Vvcxy)=\displaystyle P_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}}(V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}})= Pind​(1+‖Vvcxy‖44​Vind4−‖Vvcxy‖22​Vind2)1/2⏟induced+\displaystyle\underbrace{P_{\mathrm{ind}}\left(\sqrt{1+\frac{\|V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}}\|^{4}}{4V_{\mathrm{ind}}^{4}}}-\frac{\|V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}}\|^{2}}{2V_{\mathrm{ind}}^{2}}\right)^{1/2}}_{\text{induced}}+
P0​(1+3​‖Vvcxy‖2Vtip2)⏟blade profile+12​d0​ρ​s​A​‖Vvcxy‖3⏟parasite,\displaystyle\underbrace{P_{\mathrm{0}}\left(1+\frac{3\|V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}}\|^{2}}{V_{\mathrm{tip}}^{2}}\right)}_{\text{blade profile}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}d_{0}\rho sA\|V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}}\|^{3}}_{\text{parasite}}, (15)

where PindP_{\mathrm{ind}} and P0P_{\mathrm{0}} are the induced power during hovering and the blade profile power, respectively. Moreover, VtipV_{\mathrm{tip}} and VindV_{\mathrm{ind}} are the rotor tip speed and the mean induced velocity in hovering, respectively. In addition, d0d_{0}, ρ\rho, ss, and AA correspond to the fuselage drag ratio, air density, rotor solidity, and rotor disk area, respectively.

Moreover, for the vv-th UAV in the cc-th cluster flying with speed VvczV_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{z}} vertically, the propulsion power consumption is as follows [44]:

Pvcz​(Vvcz)={W​Vvcz,Vvcz>0,0,Vvcz≤0,P_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{z}}(V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{z}})=\begin{cases}WV_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{z}},&V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{z}}>0,\\ 0,&V_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{z}}\leq 0,\end{cases} (16)

where W=m​gW=mg is the weight of UAV, with mm being its mass and gg representing the gravitational acceleration.

Accordingly, the total flight energy consumption of the vv-th UAV in the cc-th cluster is as follows:

Evcflight=∫0T(Pvcxy+Pvcz)​𝑑t.E_{v_{c}}^{\text{flight}}=\int_{0}^{T}\left(P_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{xy}}+P_{v_{c}}^{\textrm{z}}\right)dt. (17)

where TT denotes the flight duration.

IV Problem Formulation and Analysis

In this section, we formulate the optimization problem, termed data collection and semantic forwarding muti-objective optimization problem (DCSFMOP). Initially, the decision variables, objective functions, and overall structure of the optimization problem are presented. Then, the properties and characteristics of the formulated optimization problem are analyzed.

IV-A Problem Formulation

The communication system considered in this work encompasses two distinct types of links, which are the ground user-to-UAV links and UAV cluster-to-remote BS links, respectively. In the first link type, UAVs must be spatially dispersed to conduct data collection from ground users. Conversely, the second link type necessitates a relatively compact spatial distribution among UAVs within a cluster, so that enabling the formation of a high-gain, directional main lobe aimed at the remote BS, thereby maximizing semantic communication performance. However, achieving these optimized aerial positions incurs considerable energy consumption from UAV flights. Therefore, how to achieve a balanced trade-off among three conflicting objectives, i.e., maximizing the volume of data collected from ground user, maximizing semantic communication performance between the UAV clusters and BS, and minimizing energy consumption of UAVs, is crucial for establishing an effective post-disaster communication network.

The decision variables are defined as follows. First, the UAV clustering is denoted by 𝐜=\mathbf{c}= {cv∈{1,2,…,Ncluster}\{c_{v}\in\{1,2,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{cluster}}\} |v∈𝒱}|v\in\mathcal{V}\} with cvc_{v} indicating the cluster assignment of the vv-th UAV. Second, the set of UAV locations, composed of the continuous coordinates, is denoted by 𝐐={qvc|v∈𝒱,c∈𝒞}\mathbf{Q}=\{\textbf{q}_{v_{c}}|v\in\mathcal{V},c\in\mathcal{C}\}. Third, the set of excitation current weights of UAVs is denoted by 𝐰={wv,c|v∈𝒱,c∈𝒞}\mathbf{w}=\{w_{v,c}|v\in\mathcal{V},c\in\mathcal{C}\}. Finally, the set of average number of semantic symbols used per word in each UAV cluster is denoted by 𝐤={kc,bs|c∈𝒞}\mathbf{k}=\{k_{c,\mathrm{bs}}|c\in\mathcal{C}\}. Based on these decision variables, the considered optimization objectives are detailed as follows.

In post-disaster communication scenarios, maximizing the total transmission rate of all served ground users is critical to ensure efficient and reliable data collection. Accordingly, the first optimization objective is formulated as

f1​(𝐐)=∑u=1NURu,vu⋆.f_{1}(\mathbf{Q})=\sum_{u=1}^{N_{U}}R_{u,v_{u}^{\star}}. (18)

Considering the presence of multiple UAV clusters, the second optimization objective is to maximize the total semantic transmission rate, which is defined as the amount of semantic information sent per second and is measured in suts/s, thereby enhancing the overall network capacity. Thus, the second optimization objective function is as follows:

f2​(𝐜,𝐐,𝐰,𝐤)=∑c=1NCS​Rc,bs.f_{2}(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{w},\mathbf{k})=\sum_{c=1}^{N_{C}}SR_{c,\mathrm{bs}}. (19)

Considering the limited battery capacity of UAVs and the impracticality of frequent recharging or replacement in post-disaster scenarios, the third optimization objective is to minimize the total energy consumption of all UAVs, which helps prolong the operational duration of the network and improves communication reliability. Therefore, the third objective function is defined as follows:

f3​(𝐐)=∑c=1Ncluster∑v=1NVcEvcflight.f_{3}(\mathbf{Q})=\sum_{c=1}^{N_{\mathrm{cluster}}}\sum_{v=1}^{N_{V_{c}}}E_{v_{c}}^{\text{flight}}. (20)

Accordingly, the DCSFMOP is formulated as follows:

max{𝐜,𝐐,𝐰,𝐤}\displaystyle\underset{\{\mathbf{c},\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{w},\mathbf{k}\}}{\text{max}}\ {f1,f2,−f3},\displaystyle\{f_{1},f_{2},-f_{3}\}, (21a)
s.t. C​1:𝐪vc∈ℛ,∀v∈𝒱,∀c∈𝒞,\displaystyle C1:\mathbf{q}_{v_{c}}\in\mathcal{R},\quad\forall v\in\mathcal{V},\forall c\in\mathcal{C}, (21b)
C​2:∥𝐪vici−𝐪vjcj∥≥dmin,∀vi,vj∈𝒱,vi≠vj,\displaystyle C2:\lVert\mathbf{q}_{{v_{i}}_{c_{i}}}-\mathbf{q}_{{v_{j}}_{c_{j}}}\rVert\geq d_{\textrm{min}},\quad\forall v_{i},v_{j}\in\mathcal{V},v_{i}\neq v_{j}, (21c)
C​3:NVc≥1,∀c∈{1,…,Ncluster},\displaystyle C3:N_{\mathrm{V}_{c}}\geq 1,\quad\forall c\in\{1,\dots,N_{\textrm{cluster}}\}, (21d)
C​4:cv∈{1,2,…,Ncluster},∀u∈𝒰,\displaystyle C4:c_{v}\in\{1,2,\ldots,N_{\textrm{cluster}}\},\quad\forall u\in\mathcal{U}, (21e)
C​5:∑c=1NclusterNVc=NV,\displaystyle C5:\sum_{c=1}^{N_{\textrm{cluster}}}N_{\mathrm{V}_{c}}=N_{\textrm{V}}, (21f)
C​6:ξc,bs≥ξth,∀c∈𝒞,\displaystyle C6:\xi_{c,\mathrm{bs}}\geq\xi_{\text{th}},\forall c\in\mathcal{C}, (21g)
C​7:kc,s={[kmin,kmax] if ​f1>f2not optimized if ​f1≤f2,\displaystyle C7:k_{c,s}=\begin{cases}[k_{\min},k_{\max}]\quad\text{ if }f_{1}>f_{2}\\ \textrm{not optimized}\quad\text{ if }f_{1}\leq f_{2},\end{cases} (21h)

where constraint (21b) restricts the deployment of UAVs to the predefined 3D space ℛ\mathcal{R} and constraint (21c) manifests a minimum safety distance between any two UAVs to avoid collisions. Moreover, constraint (21d) enforces that each cluster contains at least one UAV, constraint (21e) guarantees that each UAV belongs to exactly one cluster, constraint (21f) ensures that the total number of UAVs across all clusters equals the total number of available UAVs, and constraint (21g) defines the minimum semantic rate threshold ξth\xi_{\text{th}}. In addition, constraint (21h) indicates that when the total transmission rate of all served ground users f1f_{1} exceeds the total semantic transmission rate f2f_{2}, kc,bsk_{c,\mathrm{bs}} is optimized within the range [kmin,kmax][k_{\mathrm{min}},k_{\mathrm{max}}]. Conversely, when f1≤f2f_{1}\leq f_{2}, kc,bsk_{c,\mathrm{bs}} will not be optimized since semantic processing can evidently be omitted.

IV-B Problem Analysis

In this section, the formulated DCSFMOP is analyzed as follows.

(i) The formulated optimization problem in Eq. (21a) is an MINLP problem. First, the involvement of both discrete variables (clustering assignment 𝐜\mathbf{c} and semantic symbol number 𝐤\mathbf{k}) and continuous variables (UAV location 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and excitation current weight 𝐰\mathbf{w}) classifies it a mixed-integer problem. Second, the objective functions f1f_{1}, f2f_{2}, and f3f_{3} are all inherently nonlinear. Specifically, f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} apply nonlinear distance-based path loss model and f3f_{3} contains square roots, power functions, and integrals which are nonlinear. Therefore, the formulated DCSFMOP is a typical MINLP problem.

(ii) The formulated optimization problem in Eq. (21a) is NP-hard. Specifically, if 𝐐,𝐰,𝐤\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{w},\mathbf{k} are fixed, the optimization with respect to the discrete cluster assignment 𝐜\mathbf{c} reduces to allocating NVN_{V} UAVs to NclusterN_{\mathrm{cluster}} clusters, subject to the constraints that each UAV must belong to exactly one cluster and each cluster must contain at least one UAV, while aiming to maximize f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}. In this case, f2f_{2} imposes a requirement that the UAVs within each cluster maintain a compact spatial configuration to maximize the array gain. The aforementioned subproblem can be formulated as a k-means clustering problem, which is known to be NP-hard. Therefore, the subproblem is NP-hard, and consequently, the overall DCSFMOP is also NP-hard.

(iii) The formulated optimization problem in Eq. (21a) has dynamically varying dimensionality of decision variables. Specifically, the optimization of the number of semantic symbols per cluster, i.e., 𝐤\mathbf{k}, is determined by the UAV cluster assignment scheme, as the dimensionality of 𝐤\mathbf{k} can only be determined once the number of clusters is specified. Consequently, any changes in the number of UAV clusters results in a corresponding change in the dimension of 𝐤\mathbf{k}, which in turn leads to dynamically varying decision variables throughout the optimization process.

Given the aforementioned characteristics, the formulated optimization problem cannot be directly tackled by existing conventional algorithms. Therefore, we propose a dedicated approach to efficiently obtain feasible solutions.

V The Proposed Approach

In this section, we first elaborate the motivation of proposing LLM-AOA for solving the formulated problem. Then, we present the preliminaries of the proposed LLM-AOA. Finally, we introduce the detailed description of the overall LLM-AOA framework.

V-A Motivation

As presented in Section IV-B, the formulated DCSFMOP is a MINLP problem and inherently NP-hard with dynamically varying decision variable dimensionality, which renders it intractable for traditional algorithms. Specifically, DRL-based algorithms face extremely difficult state representation and action space definition when dealing with dynamic decision spaces, while convex optimization-based algorithms are generally unsuitable since the formulated problem is non-convex. In this case, AO provides an effective framework for the formulated DCSFMOP by sequentially optimizing different subsets of decision variables. First, it determines the UAV clustering assignment, which fixes the dimensionality of the remaining decision variables. Then, the remaining variables are optimized sequentially. The approach mitigates the computational complexity of jointly handling dynamically varying variables.

Different subsets of decision variables exhibit distinct mathematical properties, which necessitates tailored optimization strategies. Specifically, the UAV clustering assignment is a combinatorial problem with an exponentially growing search space, for which a greedy strategy offers an optimal trade-off between computational efficiency and solution quality. Moreover, for optimizing the number of semantic symbols, which is a low-dimensional discrete problem, a greedy strategy yields optimal or near-optimal solutions with relatively low computational overhead. Finally, evolutionary computation algorithms are suitable for the joint optimization of UAV locations and weights which is a high-dimensional, continuous, and non-convex problem [45]. However, these algorithms often struggle with premature convergence, parameter sensitivity, and inefficient exploration in complex solution spaces.

The integration of LLMs into the optimization process of evolutionary computation algorithms addresses these limitations through their advanced reasoning and analytical capabilities. LLMs offer the following advantages in our research context. First, LLMs dynamically analyze population statistics and evolutionary patterns to identify optimization states that remain undetectable through conventional metrics. Second, they also leverage transfer learning from diverse domains to propose effective parameter adjustments appropriate for different optimization phases. Finally, LLMs provide context-aware guidance that adapts to the evolving search landscape. When algorithms exhibit premature convergence, LLMs recommend increasing the value of mutation parameter or implementing diversity preservation mechanisms. Conversely, in situations of slow convergence with excessive diversity, LLMs suggest decreasing the value of mutation parameter. Such a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism enhances algorithmic navigation through the complex search space of UAV locations and weights.

According to the aforementioned motivation, we propose LLM-AOA, which synergistically integrates greedy strategy and LLM-guided evolutionary computation within the AO framework to efficiently and effectively solve the formulated DCSFMOP. In the following, some preliminaries of the proposed LLM-AOA are introduced.

V-B Preliminaries

In this section, we present the principles of the AO framework, greedy strategy, evolutionary computation, and large language model, respectively.

V-B1 AO Framework

AO decomposes a complex optimization problem into several subproblems by iteratively optimizing one subset of decision variables while keeping others fixed. Given an optimization problem f⁡(x1,…,xn)f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) with decision variables x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}, where nn is the dimension of the decision variables, the AO procedure proceeds as follows [46]:

1) Initialization. Initialize variables {xi(0)}i=1n\{x_{i}^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^{n} and set the maximum number of iterations TmaxAOT_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{AO}}.

2) Alternating Optimization. In each iteration, the variables are optimized sequentially while all other variables remain fixed. Specifically, in the tt-th iteration, x1(t)x_{1}^{(t)} is updated as follows:

x1(t)=arg⁡minx1⁡f⁡(x1,x2(t−1),…,xn(t−1)).x_{1}^{(t)}=\arg\min_{x_{1}}f(x_{1},x_{2}^{(t-1)},\ldots,x_{n}^{(t-1)}). (22)

Subsequently, x2(t)x_{2}^{(t)} is optimized as follows:

x2(t)=arg⁡minx2⁡f⁡(x1(t),x2,…,xn(t−1)).x_{2}^{(t)}=\arg\min_{x_{2}}f(x_{1}^{(t)},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}^{(t-1)}). (23)

The process continues until all decision variables are updated within the iteration.

3) Termination. The algorithm terminates when the maximum number of iterations TmaxAOT_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{AO}} is reached, yielding the final variables {xi(TmaxAO)}i=1n\{x_{i}^{(T_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{AO}})}\}_{i=1}^{n}. Alternatively, convergence-based stopping criteria can also be used, such as ‖xi(t)−xi(t−1)‖≤ϵ1\|x_{i}^{(t)}-x_{i}^{(t-1)}\|\leq\epsilon_{1} for all i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

V-B2 Greedy Strategy

The greedy strategy selects the locally optimal choice at each step based on the currently available information. The fundamental principle lies in constructing a global solution through a sequence of locally optimal decisions, under the assumption that such incremental optimization will lead to a near-optimal or optimal overall solution. Specifically, the greedy strategy is characterized by the following two properties:

1) Greedy Choice. Given an original problem ℙ\mathbb{P}, let x1x_{1} be the greedy choice made at the current step. Let ℙ′\mathbb{P}^{\prime} denote the resulting subproblem after this choice is incorporated. The greedy-choice property guarantees that there exists an optimal solution 𝐀\mathbf{A} to ℙ\mathbb{P} that can be expressed as 𝐀={x1,𝐀′}\mathbf{A}=\{x_{1},\mathbf{A}^{\prime}\}, where 𝐀′\mathbf{A}^{\prime} is an optimal solution to the subproblem ℙ′\mathbb{P}^{\prime}.

2) Optimal Substructure. Let ℙ\mathbb{P} be the original optimization problem and 𝐀\mathbf{A} be an optimal solution to ℙ\mathbb{P}. If 𝐀\mathbf{A} is composed of the current choice xx and a solution 𝐀′\mathbf{A}^{\prime} of the subproblem ℙ′\mathbb{P}^{\prime}, then 𝐀′\mathbf{A}^{\prime} must be the optimal solution of the subproblem ℙ′\mathbb{P}^{\prime}.

V-B3 Evolutionary Computation

Evolutionary computation is a class of optimization methods inspired by natural evolution and swarm intelligence. By iteratively updating a population of candidate solutions, the overall performance gradually improves [47]. Evolutionary computation is suitable for high-dimensional, non-convex, multi-objective, and complex constraint optimization problems.

The procedure of evolutionary computation algorithms is as follows. First, an initial population of candidate solutions is generated. Then, the algorithm iteratively produces new candidates, evaluates their fitness, and selects superior solutions to form the next generation. The iterative process continues until a predefined termination condition, e.g., a maximum number of iterations is satisfied, upon which the algorithm outputs an optimal or near-optimal solution.

V-B4 Large Language Model

LLMs are a class of foundation models trained on large-scale corpora, which are capable of capturing complex linguistic structures, contextual semantic relationships, and implicit high-level reasoning patterns [48]. Representative LLMs include the GPT series [49], e.g., GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, Gemini [50], and Claude, developed by OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, respectively.

The capability of LLMs to comprehend, summarize, and support decision-making on complex data enables them to assist in addressing diverse optimization problems. Specifically, LLMs can act as intelligent coordinators for optimization algorithms, which dynamically adjusts parameters and control strategies to guide the algorithms towards more efficient and effective solutions [51], [52]. For example, they can adjust reward function weights in DRL-based algorithms and tune population update rules in evolutionary computation.

V-C The Proposed LLM-AOA

Based on the aforementioned preliminaries, we propose LLM-AOA to effectively solve the formulated DCSFMOP. Inspired by evolutionary computation, LLM-AOA adopts a population-based solution representation, where each individual denotes a feasible solution. Specifically, LLM-AOA comprises an initialization phase which generates the initial population and an AO phase which evolves the population to obtain high-quality solutions.

Fig. 2 shows the framework of the proposed LLM-AOA in terms of handling the formulated DCSFMOP, which provides a visual representation of how these components are integrated. The overall structure of LLM-AOA is shown in Algorithm 1 and the details are elaborated as follows.

V-C1 Initialization Phase

During the initialization phase, LLM-AOA generates an initial population 𝒫(0)\mathcal{P}^{(0)} and sets the algorithmic parameters. Given the heterogeneous decision variables, the traditional unified initialization is infeasible. Therefore, LLM-AOA adopts a mixed initialization method to cover the diverse search space and enhance the uniformity of solution distribution. Specifically, the population size is set as MM and then the mm-th individual in 𝒫(0)\mathcal{P}^{(0)} is as follows:

𝒑m(0)={𝐜m(0),𝐐m(0),𝐰m(0),𝐤m(0)},m=1,…,M.\bm{p}_{m}^{(0)}=\{\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(0)},\mathbf{Q}_{m}^{(0)},\mathbf{w}_{m}^{(0)},\mathbf{k}_{m}^{(0)}\},\quad m=1,\ldots,M. (24)

Given the heterogeneous nature of the decision variables, i.e., 𝐜m(0)\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(0)}, 𝐐m(0)\mathbf{Q}_{m}^{(0)}, 𝐰m(0)\mathbf{w}_{m}^{(0)}, 𝐤m(0)\mathbf{k}_{m}^{(0)}, we initialize each component separately.

1) Initialization of 𝐜m(0)\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(0)}: The ii-th element [cm(0)]i[c_{m}^{(0)}]_{i} of the UAV cluster assignment vector 𝐜m(0)\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(0)} is initialized as follows:

[cm(0)]i=randint⁡(1,NV),[c_{m}^{(0)}]_{i}=\mathrm{randint}(1,N_{\mathrm{V}}), (25)

where randint⁡(1,NV)\mathrm{randint}(1,N_{\mathrm{V}}) denotes the function that selects an integer uniformly at random from the discrete set {1,…,NV}\{1,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{V}}\}.

2) Initialization of 𝐐m(0)\mathbf{Q}_{m}^{(0)}: The 3D locations of the ii-th UAV [𝐪m(0)]i[\mathbf{q}^{(0)}_{m}]_{i} in 𝐐m(0)={[𝐪m(0)]1,…,[𝐪m(0)]NV}\mathbf{Q}_{m}^{(0)}=\{[\mathbf{q}^{(0)}_{m}]_{1},\ldots,[\mathbf{q}^{(0)}_{m}]_{N_{\mathrm{V}}}\} is initialized as follows:

[𝐪m(0)]i=𝐪min+𝐫⊙(𝐪max−𝐪min),[\mathbf{q}^{(0)}_{m}]_{i}=\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{min}}+\mathbf{r}\odot(\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{max}}-\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{min}}), (26)

where 𝐫\mathbf{r} represents a 1×3 array whose elements are independently drawn from a uniform distribution over the interval [0,1][0,1] and ⊙\odot is the Hadamard (element-wise) product. The vector 𝐪min={xmin,ymin,zmin}\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{min}}=\{x_{\min},y_{\min},z_{\min}\} and 𝐪max={xmax,ymax,zmax}\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{max}}=\{x_{\max},y_{\max},z_{\max}\} define the lower and upper bounds of the 3D locations for all UAVs, respectively.

3) Initialization of 𝐰m(0)\mathbf{w}_{m}^{(0)}: The ii-th element [wm(0)]i[w_{m}^{(0)}]_{i} of the excitation current weight vector 𝐰m(0)\mathbf{w}_{m}^{(0)} is initialized as follows:

[wm(0)]i=uniform⁡(wmin,wmax),[w_{m}^{(0)}]_{i}=\mathrm{uniform}(w_{\min},w_{\max}), (27)

where uniform⁡(wmin,wmax)\mathrm{uniform}(w_{\min},w_{\max}) denotes a function that selects a real number from the continuous interval [wmin,wmax][w_{\min},w_{\max}] based on the uniform probability distribution.

4) Initialization of 𝐤m(0)\mathbf{k}_{m}^{(0)}: The ii-th element [km(0)]i[k_{m}^{(0)}]_{i} of the number of transmitted symbols of each cluster 𝐤m(0)\mathbf{k}_{m}^{(0)} is initialized by selecting a discrete integer uniformly at random from the range [kmin,kmax][k_{\min},k_{\max}], the initialization is as follows:

[km(0)]i=randint⁡(kmin,kmax).[k_{m}^{(0)}]_{i}=\mathrm{randint}(k_{\min},k_{\max}). (28)

After all the aforementioned components, i.e., 𝐜m(0)\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(0)}, 𝐐m(0)\mathbf{Q}_{m}^{(0)}, 𝐰m(0)\mathbf{w}_{m}^{(0)}, and 𝐤m(0)\mathbf{k}_{m}^{(0)}, are initialized, they are concatenated to form the mm-th individual 𝒑m(0)\bm{p}_{m}^{(0)}. The concatenation of all individuals, i.e., 𝒑1(0),…,𝒑M(0)\bm{p}_{1}^{(0)},\ldots,\bm{p}_{M}^{(0)}, forms the initial population 𝒫(0)\mathcal{P}^{(0)}. Consequently, an alternative representation of 𝒫(0)\mathcal{P}^{(0)} can be formulated as 𝒫(0)={𝐜(0),𝐐(0),𝐰(0),𝐤(0)}\mathcal{P}^{(0)}=\{\mathbf{c}^{(0)},\mathbf{Q}^{(0)},\mathbf{w}^{(0)},\mathbf{k}^{(0)}\}, where 𝐜(0)={𝐜1(0),…,𝐜M(0)}\mathbf{c}^{(0)}=\{\mathbf{c}_{1}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{c}_{M}^{(0)}\}, 𝐐(0)={𝐐1(0),…,𝐐M(0)}\mathbf{Q}^{(0)}=\{\mathbf{Q}_{1}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{Q}_{M}^{(0)}\}, 𝐰(0)={𝐰1(0),…,𝐰M(0)}\mathbf{w}^{(0)}=\{\mathbf{w}_{1}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{w}_{M}^{(0)}\}, and 𝐤(0)={𝐤1(0),…,𝐤M(0)}\mathbf{k}^{(0)}=\{\mathbf{k}_{1}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{k}_{M}^{(0)}\}.

Finally, 𝒫(0)={𝐜(0),𝐐(0),𝐰(0),𝐤(0)}\mathcal{P}^{(0)}=\{\mathbf{c}^{(0)},\mathbf{Q}^{(0)},\mathbf{w}^{(0)},\mathbf{k}^{(0)}\} is input to the AO phase for further optimization.

V-C2 AO Phase

During the optimization phase, we use the AO framework to address the varying decision variables dimensionality. Specifically, the decision variables are decomposed into three components, i.e., 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}, 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} as well as 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)}, and 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)}. Accordingly, the overall AO process is systematically structured into four sequential stages. In AO stage 1, 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)} is optimized by a greedy strategy-based algorithm. In AO stage 2, 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} are optimized via an evolutionary computation algorithm which is assisted by LLM. In AO stage 3, 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)} is determined by using another greedy strategy-based algorithm. Finally, in AO stage 4, comprehensive assessment is conducted to filter superior solutions. The details of the AO phase are presented as follows.

1) AO Stage 1: Optimization of 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}: The optimization of 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)} is a combinatorial optimization problem whose solution space grows exponentially with the number of UAVs increasing. Compared with exhaustive search or conventional evolutionary algorithms, a greedy strategy achieves high-quality solutions with significantly lower computational overhead. Therefore, in this stage, 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)} is optimized by the proposed GCA, while the other decision variables, i.e., 𝐐(t−1)\mathbf{Q}^{(t-1)}, 𝐰(t−1)\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}, and 𝐤(t−1)\mathbf{k}^{(t-1)}, are fixed. Specifically, the proposed GCA iteratively optimizes the UAV cluster assignment of each individual in the population, i.e., 𝐜1(t),…,𝐜M(t)\mathbf{c}_{1}^{(t)},\ldots,\mathbf{c}_{M}^{(t)}. The algorithm is presented in Algorithm 2 and the involved initialization and greedy iterative processes are elaborated as follows.

During the initialization process, the proposed GCA initializes the cluster assignment, constructs the set of clusters, and declares the control variables for the forthcoming greedy iterative process.

First, the proposed GCA initializes the cluster assignment of the current iteration as 𝐜m(t)←𝐜m(t−1)\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(t)}\leftarrow\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(t-1)}, where 𝐜m(t)={c1(t),c2(t),…,cNV(t)}\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(t)}=\{c_{1}^{(t)},c^{(t)}_{2},\ldots,c_{N_{\mathrm{V}}}^{(t)}\}.

Subsequently, the total number of UAV clusters in 𝐜m(t)\mathbf{c}_{m}^{(t)} is determined by the maximum cluster index as follows:

Ncluster(t)=max⁡(c1(t),c2(t),…,cNV(t)),N^{(t)}_{\mathrm{cluster}}=\mathrm{max}\left(c^{(t)}_{1},c^{(t)}_{2},\ldots,c^{(t)}_{N_{\mathrm{V}}}\right), (29)

where max⁡(⋅)\mathrm{max}(\cdot) returns the maximum value among the elements in the input set. Based on the calculated Ncluster(t)N^{(t)}_{\mathrm{cluster}}, the set of UAV clusters in the tt-th iteration, denoted by 𝒞(t)\mathscr{C}^{(t)}, is initialized as 𝒞(t)={𝒞1(t),𝒞2(t),…,𝒞Ncluster(t)(t)}\mathscr{C}^{(t)}=\{\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{1},\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{N^{(t)}_{\mathrm{cluster}}}\}. Initially, each element in 𝒞t\mathscr{C}^{t} is set to the empty set ∅\varnothing. Then, each element of 𝒞(t)\mathscr{C}^{(t)} is initialized. For example, the set of 𝒞i(t)\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{i}, which contains the indices of all UAVs belonging to the ii-th cluster, is set as 𝒞i(t)={j∣cj(t)=i, 1≤j≤NV}\mathcal{C}^{(t)}_{i}=\left\{j\mid c^{(t)}_{j}=i,\ 1\leq j\leq N_{\text{V}}\right\};

Finally, the proposed GCA initializes a boolean variable continue=TRUE\texttt{continue}=\texttt{TRUE} to regulate the iterative execution of the subsequent greedy process.

During the greedy iterative process, the proposed GCA searches over all cluster pairs to identify the merge operation which yields the greatest enhancement in the objective function f2f_{2}.

First, several auxiliary parameters are declared. Specifically, the benefit gain f2gainf^{\mathrm{gain}}_{2} of f2f_{2} in the current loop is initialized to −∞-\infty and the set of cluster pairs yielding the maximum merging gain is defined as 𝐜merge\mathbf{c}_{\mathrm{merge}}.

Subsequently, clusters are iteratively merged in a pairwise manner. Specifically, for each candidate pair of clusters indexed by bb and b′b^{\prime}, a temporary cluster set 𝒞temp\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}} is constructed based on the current 𝒞(t)\mathscr{C}^{(t)}. The merging operation incorporates the b′b^{\prime}-th cluster 𝒞b′temp\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{b^{\prime}} into the bb-th cluster 𝒞btemp\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{b} via 𝒞btemp←𝒞btemp​⋃𝒞b′temp\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{b}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{b}\bigcup\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{b^{\prime}}, after which the redundant b′b^{\prime}-th cluster 𝒞b′temp\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{b^{\prime}} is removed from 𝒞temp\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}} by 𝒞temp=𝒞temp∖𝒞b′temp\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}=\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}\setminus\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{b^{\prime}}. In the following, the cluster labels are then readjusted to ensure that all indices are consecutive integers. For example, assuming 𝒞temp={𝒞1temp,𝒞2temp,𝒞3temp}\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}=\{\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{1},\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{2},\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{3}\}, in this case, if 𝒞1temp\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{1} and 𝒞2temp\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{2} are merged, the elements in 𝒞temp\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}} will be adjusted as 𝒞temp={𝒞1temp,𝒞2temp}\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}=\{\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{1},\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{2}\}. Following the reorganization, 𝐜temp\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{temp}} is updated based on 𝒞temp\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{temp}}, and the corresponding objective function value f2tempf^{\mathrm{temp}}_{2} is calculated. The algorithm then evaluates whether f2temp−[f2]m(t−1)f^{\mathrm{temp}}_{2}-[{f_{2}}]_{m}^{(t-1)} exceeds f2gainf^{\mathrm{gain}}_{2}. If this condition is satisfied, indicating that merging the bb-th and b′b^{\prime}-th clusters provides a superior benefit, the algorithm updates 𝐜merge={b,b′}\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{merge}}=\{b,b^{\prime}\} and revises the gain metric as follows:

f2gain=f2temp−[f2]m(t−1).f^{\mathrm{gain}}_{2}=f_{2}^{\mathrm{temp}}-[{f_{2}}]_{m}^{(t-1)}. (30)

Finally, following the evaluation of all potential cluster pairs, the GCA determines whether to perform a merge operation based on the auxiliary parameter f2gainf^{\mathrm{gain}}_{2}. If f2gain>0f^{\mathrm{gain}}_{2}>0, indicating that a beneficial merging exists, the algorithm proceeds with the optimal merger in 𝐜merge\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{merge}}. Specifically, the algorithm extracts the corresponding cluster indices bb and b′b^{\prime} from 𝐜merge\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{merge}}, incorporates the b′b^{\prime}-th cluster into the bb-th cluster, removes the b′b^{\prime}-th cluster from 𝒞(t)\mathscr{C}^{(t)}, renumbers the remaining clusters in 𝒞(t)\mathscr{C}^{(t)}, and updates 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)} based on the merged cluster set 𝒞(t)\mathscr{C}^{(t)}. Conversely, if f2gain≤0f^{\mathrm{gain}}_{2}\leq 0, the Boolean variable continue is set to false, and the GCA terminates.

Based on the aforementioned GCA, 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)} is optimized. The optimized 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}, along with 𝐐(t−1)\mathbf{Q}^{(t-1)}, 𝐰(t−1)\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}, and 𝐤(t−1)\mathbf{k}^{(t-1)} from the previous iteration, are then input to AO Stage 2 for the optimization of 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} in current iteration.

2) AO Stage 2: Optimization of 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)}: The joint optimization of 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} forms a high-dimensional, continuous, and non-convex problem. Evolutionary computation algorithms are well suited to handle the problem, as their population-based global search enables effective exploration of high-dimensional spaces and facilitates the discovery of optimal or near-optimal solutions. However, traditional evolutionary computation algorithms suffer from two main limitations, which are premature convergence and inefficient static parameter settings. To address these issues, we integrate an LLM with evolutionary computation algorithms to dynamically adjust algorithmic parameters based on population statistics. Specifically, by providing context-aware parameter tuning, the LLM can enhance the performance of evolutionary computation algorithms. Thus, in this stage, we integrate NSGA-II, which is the commonly used evolutionary computation algorithm, with an LLM to achieve the joint optimization of 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} while maintaining 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)} and 𝐤(t−1)\mathbf{k}^{(t-1)} as fixed parameters. The structure of the LLM-guided NSGA-II is presented in Algorithm 3 and the corresponding initialization and evolutionary optimization processes are elaborated as follows.

During the initialization process, the algorithm first sets its operational parameters, including the maximum number of local iterations TlocalT_{\mathrm{local}}, the crossover probability pcp_{\mathrm{c}}, and the mutation probability pmp_{\mathrm{m}}. Moreover, a temporary population 𝒫temp\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}} is initialized.

During the evolutionary process, NSGA-II evolves the population through TlocalT_{\mathrm{local}} generations, sequentially applying crossover and mutation operations in each generation to produce offspring individuals.

In each generation, NSGA-II first performs a crossover operation to generate ncross=pc​Mn_{\mathrm{cross}}=p_{\mathrm{c}}M offspring individuals. Specifically, an offspring population 𝒫cross\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cross}} is initialized as an empty set. The algorithm then performs ncross/2n_{\mathrm{cross}}/2 crossover operations, where each operation selects two parent solutions 𝒑1\bm{p}_{1} and 𝒑2\bm{p}_{2} from 𝒫temp\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}}. The crossover operations are applied specifically to 𝐐(t−1)\mathbf{Q}^{(t-1)} and 𝐰(t−1)\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)} of both parents, so that generating two offspring solutions 𝒑1′\bm{p}_{1}^{\prime} and 𝒑2′\bm{p}_{2}^{\prime}. These offspring solutions are then added to the crossover population 𝒫cross\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cross}}.

Following crossover, mutation operations are applied to introduce additional diversity into the population. Specifically, the following mutation operation begins by calculating the number of mutation operations as nmut=pm​Mn_{\mathrm{mut}}=p_{\mathrm{m}}M. An empty mutation population 𝒫mut\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{mut}} is initialized to store the mutated solutions. For each of the nmutn_{\mathrm{mut}} operations, a parent 𝒑\bm{p} is randomly selected from the 𝒫temp\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}}. Mutation operations are applied to 𝐐(t−1)\mathbf{Q}^{(t-1)} and 𝐰(t−1)\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}, so that generating a mutated solution 𝒑′\bm{p}^{\prime}. The mutated solution is then added to the mutation population 𝒫mut\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{mut}}.

After generating crossover and mutation offspring, the algorithm performs a selection step to retain high-quality and diverse individuals. The process begins by merging the temporary population with both the crossover and mutation populations, expressed as 𝒫temp←𝒫temp∪𝒫cross∪𝒫mut\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}}\cup\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{cross}}\cup\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{mut}}. The algorithm then evaluates the objective functions for all solutions in 𝒫temp\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}}. Next, all individuals in 𝒫temp\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}} are ranked by non-dominated sorting to identify Pareto fronts. For each front, the crowding distance is computed to preserve population diversity, and dominated individuals are subsequently truncated to maintain a constant population size MM.

After selection, the algorithm introduces LLM to conduct parameter adjustment11 1 The related code for adjusting algorithm optimization parameters by using LLMs in the MATLAB platform can be found in: https://github.com/xiaoya257248/LLMs_generated-parameters. Specifically, this process calculates the SP and M3∗M_{3}^{*} metrics for the current Pareto front [53]. These metrics, along with relevant population data, are sent to an LLM. Based on these information, the LLM analyzes the optimization state and generates recommendations to adjust parameter values, i.e., the crossover probability pcp_{c} and mutation probability pmp_{m}. For example, if the SP metric indicates poor distribution of solutions and the M3∗M_{3}^{*} metric shows limited spread, the LLM might recommend increasing the mutation probability to promote exploration. The response of LLM is parsed to extract the recommended parameter values, which are then used for the next generation of the evolutionary process.

Upon completion of all TlocalT_{\mathrm{local}} iterations of the evolution process, the algorithm returns 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} of 𝒫temp\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{temp}} as 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)} and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)}. These optimized parameters, along with 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)} and 𝐤(t−1)\mathbf{k}^{(t-1)} are then input to AO Stage 3 for the optimization of 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)} in current iteration.

3) AO Stage 3: Optimization of 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)}: Once 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}, 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)}, and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} are fixed, optimizing 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)} becomes a low-dimensional discrete problem, as clusters can be optimized independently. Compared with dynamic programming, which incurs unnecessary computational overhead, and evolutionary computation, which requires extensive fitness evaluations, a greedy-based strategy can efficiently obtain the optimal solution with lower computational complexity. Thus, we propose GSO to optimize 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)} in this stage, while keeping 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}, 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)}, and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} fixed. Similarly, the proposed GSO iteratively optimizes the number of semantic symbols per UAV cluster of each individual in the population, i.e., 𝐤1(t),…,𝐤M(t)\mathbf{k}_{1}^{(t)},\ldots,\mathbf{k}_{M}^{(t)}. The structure of the proposed GSO is presented in Algorithm 4 and the detailed processes are as follows.

The GSO initializes the 𝐤m(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)}_{m} via assigning 𝐤m(t−1)\mathbf{k}^{(t-1)}_{m} to it and calculates the total number of clusters based on Eq. (29).

Subsequently, the algorithm optimizes the number of semantic symbols [km(t)]i[k^{(t)}_{m}]_{i} for each cluster i∈{1,…,Ncluster(t)}i\in\{1,\ldots,N^{(t)}_{\mathrm{cluster}}\}, while keeping all other semantic symbols fixed. The process aims to maximize the objective function f2f_{2}. To this end, several variables are initialized. Specifically, the best benefit of f2f_{2}, denoted as [f2best]i[f_{2}^{\mathrm{best}}]_{i}, is initialized as −∞-\infty and the corresponding best number of symbols [kmbest]i[k^{\mathrm{best}}_{m}]_{i} is set as [km(t)]i[k^{(t)}_{m}]_{i}. Moreover, a temporary vector 𝐤mtemp\mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{m} is defined as a copy of 𝐤m(t)\mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{(t)}}_{m}. The GSO then evaluates a candidate integer kk for the ii-th cluster, where kk is drawn from the feasible range [kmin,kmax][k_{\min},k_{\max}]. The [kmtemp]i[k^{\mathrm{temp}}_{m}]_{i} is set to kk, and the resulting second objective function value, f2tempf_{2}^{\mathrm{temp}}, is calculated based on the fixed variables (𝐜m(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}_{m}, 𝐐m(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)}_{m}, 𝐰m(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)}_{m}), and 𝐤mtemp\mathbf{k}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{m}. If the calculated f2tempf_{2}^{\mathrm{temp}} exceeds the recorded best benefit [f2best]i[f_{2}^{\mathrm{best}}]_{i}, it can be concluded that kk is better than [kmbest]i[k^{\mathrm{best}}_{m}]_{i}. Accordingly, the auxiliary variable [f2best]i[f_{2}^{\mathrm{best}}]_{i} is defined as f2tempf^{\mathrm{temp}}_{2} and [kmbest]i[k^{\mathrm{best}}_{m}]_{i} is set as kk. After evaluating all possible values of kk, the number of semantic symbols [km(t)]i[k^{(t)}_{m}]_{i} of the ii-th cluster is updated to its best-performing value [kmbest]i[k^{\mathrm{best}}_{m}]_{i}.

Finally, GSO returns the optimized 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)}. The updated 𝐤(t)\mathbf{k}^{(t)} are integrated with the previously optimized 𝐜(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}, 𝐐(t)\mathbf{Q}^{(t)}, and 𝐰(t)\mathbf{w}^{(t)} to form the current population 𝒫(t)\mathcal{P}^{(t)}, which is then input into AO Stage 4 for comprehensive assessment.

4) AO Stage 4: Assessment: All individuals in 𝒫(t)\mathcal{P}^{(t)} are first categorized by using non-dominated sorting, followed by the calculation of crowding distance to maintain diversity. Subsequently, the population is ranked based on the calculated crowding distance to establish a dominance hierarchy. If the population size 𝒫(t)\mathcal{P}^{(t)} exceeds the predefined limit MM, the population is truncated by retaining only the top MM individuals according to this dominance hierarchy, which then form the starting population for the subsequent iteration 𝒫(t+1)\mathcal{P}^{(t+1)}.

V-C3 Complexity Analysis

In this part, we analyze the complexity of the proposed LLM-AOA. Specifically, the analysis is conducted from the following three aspects:

  • •

    Complexity of the GCA: The while loop can execute a maximum number of NV−1N_{\text{V}}-1 iterations before potentially converging to a single cluster. During the tt-th iteration, let the current number of clusters be Kt=|𝒞(t)|K_{t}=|\mathscr{C}^{(t)}|, then the GCA examines Kt​(Kt−1)K_{t}(K_{t}-1) potential cluster pairs for merging. For each merge operation, the GCA performs NVN_{\text{V}} operations in the worst case for cluster re-indexing. Therefore, the overall computational complexity of the GCA can be expressed as 𝒪⁡((NV−1)⋅M⋅Kt2⋅NV)\mathcal{O}\left((N_{\text{V}}-1)\cdot M\cdot K_{t}^{2}\cdot N_{\text{V}}\right). In the worst-case scenario where KtK_{t} approaches NVN_{\text{V}}, the complexity of GCA is 𝒪⁡(M⋅NV4)\mathcal{O}(M\cdot N_{\text{V}}^{4}).

  • •

    Complexity of the LLM-guided NSGA-II: The computational complexity of the LLM-guided NSGA-II is dominated by non-dominated sorting with complexity 𝒪⁡(M2)\mathcal{O}(M^{2}) and crowding distance calculation with complexity 𝒪⁡(M​log⁡M)\mathcal{O}(M\log M) [54]. Since the non-dominated sorting operation has the higher complexity, the overall computational complexity of the LLM-guided NSGA-II is 𝒪⁡(Tlocal​M2)\mathcal{O}(T_{\mathrm{local}}M^{2}).

  • •

    Complexity of the GSO: The complexity of GSO mainly depends on the loop. The intermediate for-loop executes Ncluster(t)N^{(t)}_{\mathrm{cluster}} iterations and the inner for-loop iterates through all possible values between kmink_{\mathrm{min}} and kmaxk_{\mathrm{max}}, resulting in Krange=kmax−kmin+1K_{\text{range}}=k_{\mathrm{max}}-k_{\mathrm{min}}+1 iterations. Given that Ncluster(t)N^{(t)}_{\mathrm{cluster}} upper-bounded by NVN_{\mathrm{V}} and KrangeK_{\text{range}} is a constant, the complexity of the GSO can be written as 𝒪⁡(M⋅NV)\mathcal{O}(M\cdot N_{\mathrm{V}}).

In conclusion, the complexity of the proposed LLM-AOA is simplified as 𝒪⁡(TmaxAO⋅M⋅(NV4+Tlocal⋅M))\mathcal{O}\left(T_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{AO}}\cdot M\cdot(N_{\text{V}}^{4}+T_{\mathrm{local}}\cdot M)\right).

VI Simulation

In this section, we present simulation results to illustrate the performance of the proposed LLM-AOA in solving the formulated problem.

VI-A Simulation Setup

VI-A1 Scenario Setup

In this work, the number of ground users NUN_{\mathrm{U}} and UAVs NVN_{\mathrm{V}} are set as 500 and 8, respectively. Specifically, the locations of the ground users are defined over a 10001000 m ×\times 1000 m area and UAVs are constrained to fly at altitudes ranging from 60 m to 120 m above this area. Moreover, the location of the remote BS is set at (5000, 5000, 0) m.

VI-A2 Parameter Setup

The maximum numbers of AO iterations TmaxAOT_{\mathrm{max}}^{\mathrm{AO}} and LLM-guided NSGA-II TlocalT_{\mathrm{local}} are 50 and 10, respectively. The population size MM is set as 30 and the initial crossover as well as mutation probabilities are set as 0.8 and 0.4, respectively, which follows common practices in evolutionary computation to balance exploitation and exploration. Moreover, the transmit powers of each ground user PuP_{u} and each UAV PvP_{v} are both set as 0.1 w [55]. The wavelength λ\lambda, frequency ff, bandwidth BB, and noise power density N0N_{0} are set to 0.125 m, 2.4 MHz, 2 MHz [55], and -174dBm/Hz [56], respectively. The lower kmink_{\mathrm{min}} and upper bound kmaxk_{\mathrm{max}} of the average number of semantic symbols are set as 1 and 20 [22], respectively. In addition, the parametersof the channel model, i.e., ψ\psi, β\beta, μLoS\mu_{\mathrm{LoS}}, and μNLoS\mu_{\mathrm{NLoS}}, are set to 9.61, 0.16, 1.6 dB, and 20 dB, respectively. Finally, the adopted LLM is ChatGPT 5.0.

VI-B Visualization Results of the Proposed LLM-AOA

Fig. 3 demonstrates the spatial distribution of UAVs and their coverage for ground users in a 1000 m ×\times 1000 m area. Specifically, different color-coded asterisks represent ground users covered by different UAVs and the labeled UAV icons indicate the placements of all UAVs deployed to optimize coverage. Moreover, UAVs belonging to the same cluster are indicated by circles of the same color, whereas those without circular markers are independent UAVs that do not form clusters with others.

As can be observed, the deployed UAVs exhibit an overall balanced ground user coverage, though UAV 7 is an exception. The pattern arises from the computational capabilities and comparable communication resource limits among the deployed UAVs, under which balanced user coverage ensures uniform resource utilization and mitigates potential bottlenecks due to load imbalance. Moreover, we find that there are two different transmission strategies, which are collaborative and independent transmission, respectively. To be specific, UAVs 1, 2, and 3 form a cluster, while UAVs 4 and 6 constitute another. Within each cluster, data sharing and CB are employed to enhance signal gain and transmission efficiency. In contrast, UAVs 5, 7, and 8 operate separately, which indicates that collaborative transmission does not usually yield superior performance gains for all UAVs. Finally, the spatial distribution of UAVs exhibits two significant characteristics. On the one hand, most UAVs are deployed at or near the geometric centers of their served ground users. Such deployment feature aligns with the min–max distance principle which minimizes the maximum user-to-UAV distance, so that ensuring link quality for edge users and improving the service quality. On the other hand, UAVs engaged in collaborative transmission tend to converge toward a common geometric center, as can be observed from the locations of UAVs 1, 2, and 3. The reason is that relatively compact deployment of collaborative UAVs facilitates higher beamforming gain. The aforementioned spatial distribution of UAVs reflects a trade-off between enhancing the service quality of ground users and improving collaborative transmission efficiency.

VI-C Comparison of the Proposed LLM-AOA with Other Benchmarks

We introduce several benchmarks to make comparisons with the proposed LLM-AOA, which are multi-objective differential evolution (MODE) [57], multi-objective evolutionary algorithm based on decomposition (MOEA/D) [58], multi-objective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) [59], NSGA-II, and AOA without the assistance of LLM, respectively.

Fig. 4 illustrates the Pareto solution distributions obtained by the proposed LLM-AOA and other different benchmarks in addressing the formulated DCSFMOP. It is evident that the solutions obtained by the proposed LLM-AOA are closer to the direction of Pareto front (PF), which implies that the performance of LLM-AOA is superior to the other adopted swarm intelligence algorithms. Moreover, the numerical results in Fig. 5 further confirm this conclusion since the proposed LLM-AOA achieves the highest transmission rate, i.e., 1.10×1081.10\times 10^{8} bps, and semantic rate, i.e., 4.12×1064.12\times 10^{6} suts/s, while maintaining reasonable energy consumption. Under comparable energy consumption levels, LLM-AOA achieves approximately 26.8% and 22.9% improvements in the performance of transmission rate and semantic rate, respectively, compared with the conventional AOA. The enhanced performance can be attributed to the fact that the proposed LLM-AOA employs different schemes tailored to the specific characteristics of different components of decision variables, which allows for more effective optimization of each decision variable component and enables LLM-AOA to navigate the complex solution space more efficiently than other algorithms, resulting in better quality solutions.

VI-D Performance Evaluation of the Proposed LLM-AOA under Different Numbers of UAVs

To further verify the effectiveness of the proposed LLM-AOA in solving the formulated problem and to elucidate the impact of the number of UAVs on system performance, we extend the simulation by evaluating the performance of the proposed LLM-AOA and other benchmarks under 4, 12, and 16 UAVs, respectively.

Fig. 6 demonstrates the optimization results of different objective functions for the proposed LLM-AOA and other benchmarks under the aforementioned three different networks sizes. As can be observed, although the proposed LLM-AOA yields marginally higher values for f2f_{2} and f3f_{3} in certain scenarios, it achieves a more favorable balance among all optimization objectives, which demonstrates its superior optimization capabilities. Moreover, as the number of UAVs increases, the values of f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} exhibit an approximately linear growth tendency, which indicates that enlarging the scale of UAV network can substantially enhance the data collection and forwarding capabilities. Conversely, f3f_{3} exhibits a distinctly different pattern. Specifically, the majority of benchmarks present a substantial increase in energy consumption when the number of UAVs is expanded from 12 to 16 elements, with energy consumption surpassing 2×1052\times 10^{5}. Such phenomenon indicates a considerable deterioration in energy efficiency as the network scales beyond certain thresholds. In conclusion, in the considered system, deploying 8 or 12 UAVs offers a more favorable balance among data collection, forwarding performance, and energy consumption, thereby achieving a more desirable trade-off between system performance and energy efficiency.

VI-E Performance Evaluation of the Proposed LLM-AOA under Different LLMs

To evaluate the impact of different LLMs on optimization performance, we conduct extensive simulations by integrating five LLMs into the proposed LLM-AOA, which are ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Grok, and Qwen, respectively.

Fig. 7 illustrates the solution distributions obtained by the proposed LLM-AOA with the aforementioned LLMs and AOA. It can be observed that most LLMs which are integrated into LLM-AOA can deliver favorable performance. The only exception is Grok, for which a small fraction of solutions falls below the performance of the AOA. Moreover, different LLMs exhibit distinct tendencies in balancing the considered multiple optimization objectives. Specifically, LLM-AOA with ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek prefers more balanced parameter adjustments, achieving favorable trade-offs among semantic rate, transmission rate, and energy consumption. In contrast, LLM-AOA with Qwen prioritizes semantic rate, which yields higher semantic rate at the expense of relatively lower ground user–to–UAV transmission rates, which reflects a more aggressive single-objective preference. Finally, the solution set produced by Grok is relatively scattered, with some solutions are superior to the AOA, which suggests its limited effectiveness in handling complex multi-objective trade-offs in the considered scenario.

VII Conclusion

In this work, we have designed a low-altitude multi-UAV-assisted data collection and semantic forwarding communication network architecture for post-disaster relief. In the proposed architecture, UAVs first collect data from ground users, adaptively form different clusters, perform intra-cluster data aggregation with semantic extraction, and then cooperate as VAAs to transmit the key data to a remote BS. We have formulated a DCSFMOP, which is a MINLP problem that is inherently NP-hard and characterized by dynamically varying decision variable dimensionality. Considering the inherent characteristics of the formulated problem, we have proposed an LLM-AOA which optimizes different subsets of decision variables through tailored optimization strategies. Simulation results have demonstrated the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed LLM-AOA. Moreover, the solutions obtained by most LLMs achieve favorable performance, except for a subset of solutions obtained by Grok. In addition, LLM-AOA with ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek tends to promote balanced parameter adjustments, thereby yielding well-distributed trade-offs among the three objectives. In contrast, the LLM-AOA with Qwen emphasizes the optimization of a single objective. The aforementioned observations indicate that different LLMs exhibit distinct preferences in balancing multiple optimization objectives.

In the future, we aim to extend this research by investigating solar-powered UAV clustering in dynamic environments, exploring multi-modal semantic-driven self-organizing cluster formation, and developing distributed collaboration frameworks for heterogeneous UAV semantic communication networks to further enhance system robustness and efficiency in complex post-disaster scenarios.
